# Confidently wrong [10 min]{.time} {#confidently-wrong}

::: notes
**Goal.** By the end, everyone can say why a confident tone proves nothing and can name the five steps of the check, which is all Lab Three needs.

**Have ready.** The Case A block, to paste into the chat from its own slide. The plan slide's vote shows who has the Lab One practice output saved with its PRACTICE OUTPUT line at the top; a fresh one takes two minutes, so whoever typed 2 makes it when Lab Three opens. Ask everyone to keep one output from Day One or Two, not the Lab Three one, for the end-of-day check.

**Clock.** 0:00 voice. 0:40 lane. 1:30 five steps. 2:50 kinds. 3:30 Case A. 4:00 claims. 6:20 marks. 7:20 omission. 7:50 sources. 9:20 stakes.

**Watch for.** "It has citations" heard as "verified". Could-not-find drifting into "probably fine". Someone in the chat proposing a second tool "to double-check": send them to the ladder. A real patient story typed into the chat: stop it before the detail and go back to the card. Running long: shorten the stakes slide before you shorten the lab.

**If asked.** Can the tool check its own answer? It can list claims (the last slide has the prompt); it cannot be the check. How often is it wrong? No number would apply to your tool on your task, so quote none; even the strongest accuracy score reported on Day Two was short of the maximum. Does a literature-grounded tool solve this? It gives you something to open; you still open it and read the line it supports.

**Bridge.** "You have five steps and a card. Now see whether they catch an error you did not plant: in Lab Three you swap your Lab One output with a partner."
:::

## Same voice, right or wrong {#tone-not-signal}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[A reference that exists]{.t}

::: {.nextword}
::: {.row}
[sounds sure]{.w} []{.fill style="width:7em"}
:::
:::
:::
::: {.card}
[A reference made up]{.t}

::: {.nextword}
::: {.row}
[sounds sure]{.w} []{.fill style="width:7em"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

[▲ Same voice, same bar. Nothing in the tone tells you which one is real.]{.pointer}

[Tone is not a signal. A verification step is.]{.big}

[Illustrative picture, drawn for this course]{.illustrative}

::: notes
**0:40.** Days One and Two were about getting good output. Today is the other half of the rule: a draft is only as safe as the check you put behind it. The tool writes a made-up citation in the same steady voice it uses for a correct one, so there is no hesitation to listen for. You will hear the word hallucination elsewhere; say it once, then say what happened: something invented, omitted or altered, or a citation fabricated. The bars are the same length on purpose.

**Do.** Point at the two bars, then at the last line. No chat on this slide.
:::

## Between the draft and the use {#check-lane}

::: {.lane}
[Draft with AI]{.node .dark .fixed} [→]{.op} [Cross-check the source]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [Confirm or correct]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [Use]{.node .out .fixed}
:::

::: {.lane}
[Step 2: could not find it]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Treat as wrong]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Step 3: correct it, or delete it]{.node .change .grow}
:::

[▲ Steps 2 and 3 are where you decide. Could-not-find counts as wrong.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**0:50.** What separates a right answer from a wrong one is a step you do yourself between the draft and the use: Draft with AI, Cross-check the source, Confirm or correct, then Use. The two middle steps are where you decide. And if you cannot find the source, treat the claim as wrong, then correct it or delete it.

**Do.** Point at steps 2 and 3, then trace the second lane with your cursor. No chat on this slide.
:::

## Five steps, every time {#verify-five-moves}

::: {.flow}
::: {.step}
[1]{.num} Extract every claim
:::
::: {.step}
[2]{.num} Find each source yourself
:::
::: {.step}
[3]{.num} Mark each claim
:::
::: {.step}
[4]{.num} Fix it, or discard it
:::
::: {.step}
[5]{.num} Name the error
:::
:::

[▲ Step 3 has three marks. Could-not-find counts as wrong.]{.pointer}

[✓ Confirmed]{.pill .teal} [✗ Wrong]{.pill .red} [? Could not find: treat as wrong]{.pill}

::: notes
**1:20.** This is the whole method, and Lab Three uses only this. One: pull out every checkable claim, anything a colleague could answer with "says who?": numbers, names, citations, dates, doses, guideline references. Two: find each source yourself; never ask the tool to confirm itself, because "are you sure?" returns the same voice. Three: mark each claim confirmed, wrong or could-not-find; could-not-find counts as wrong. Then read the source against the output once, for what was left out. Four: fix it, or discard the output if the errors run all through it. Five: name the kind of error. On Day One the three questions ended with a rule: "If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept." These five steps are what slowing down looks like.

**Do.** Point at each step as you say it. No chat; the next slide names the kinds of error.
:::

## Four ways it goes wrong {#error-kinds}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Invented]{.t}

[Source: A B]{.node .same}

[Output: A B C]{.node .change}

Added. Not in the source.
:::
::: {.card}
[Omitted]{.t}

[Source: A B C]{.node .same}

[Output: A B]{.node .change}

Dropped. It was in the source.
:::
::: {.card}
[Altered]{.t}

[Source: A B C]{.node .same}

[Output: A B X]{.node .change}

A value, negation, side, date or unit changed.
:::
::: {.card}
[Fabricated citation]{.t}

[Source: no such paper]{.node .ghost}

[Output: cites it]{.node .red}

Looks real. Is not, or does not say that.
:::
:::

[▲ Step 5 of the check: say which one it is.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**0:40.** Step five is naming the error, in these words. Invented: added, not in the source. Omitted: dropped, though it was in the source. Altered: a value, negation, side, date or unit changed. Or a fabricated citation: a reference that looks real and is not, or does not say what it is cited for. The letters are only a picture: the source holds some things, and the output differs from it in one way.

**Do.** Read the four cards left to right, pointing at the ringed box on each. No chat on this slide.
:::

[]{.chk} Headaches are now more frequent

[]{.chk} New ankle swelling

[]{.chk} Home BP averages 146/92

[]{.chk} Add losartan 50 mg daily, continue amlodipine

[]{.chk} Review in 6 weeks

[]{.chk} "This follows current guidelines"
:::

:::

::: notes
**2:20.** A tool was given the Case A card and asked for a short summary for a colleague. This is what came back, one claim to a row: written for this course and not captured from a real tool. The card in the chat is the source. Everyone picks one claim, finds it on the card, marks it confirmed, wrong or could-not-find, and types the claim with the mark. Do not reveal anything yet. Read out five or six answers, grouped by mark, and ask how each person found the line on the card.

**Do.** Chat · 2 min. Take one claim yourself on the shared screen as they take theirs. If the chat is quiet, take the first ("52-year-old man") and mark it. Only the card: if someone starts describing a real patient, stop them before any detail and go back to the card.
:::

## What the check finds {#case-a-key}

::: {.tight}

| | In the summary | On the card | Result |
|:----:|----------------------------------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| []{.chk .on} | 52-year-old man with hypertension, amlodipine 5 mg daily, 6 weeks | Same | Confirmed |
| []{.chk .no} | Headaches more frequent | Less frequent | Wrong: altered |
| []{.chk .on} | New ankle swelling | Same | Confirmed |
| []{.chk .on} | Home BP averages 146/92 | Same | Confirmed |
| []{.chk .on} | Add losartan 50 mg, continue amlodipine | Same | Confirmed |
| []{.chk .no} | Review in 6 weeks | Review in 4 weeks | Wrong: altered |
| []{.chk .no} | "Follows current guidelines" | No guideline named | Could-not-find: treat as wrong |

:::

[▲ Two altered values. One claim with no source.]{.pointer}

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}

::: notes
**1:00.** Three lines fail. The summary says headaches are more frequent; the card says less frequent: altered. It says review in 6 weeks; the card says 4: altered. "Follows current guidelines" names no guideline and the card has none: could-not-find, so wrong until someone names it and opens it. The other four check out: the patient line, the swelling, the home readings and the losartan line. One more finding comes from no line of the output, and it is on the next slide.

**Do.** Read the table out row by row, pointing at each box. No chat; keep it brisk.
:::

## What no line shows {#case-a-omitted}

::: {.lane}
[On the card: repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [In the summary: nothing]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Omitted]{.node .red .fixed}
:::

[▲ Omissions only show up when you read the source against the output.]{.pointer}

Step 4, fix it: [correct the two values]{.pill .teal} [restore the blood test]{.pill .teal} [delete the unsupported sentence]{.pill .teal}

::: notes
**0:30.** One finding comes from no line of the output. The card plans a repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks, and the summary never says so: that is omitted. It only shows when you read the source against the output, once, for what was left out. Then step four: correct the two values, restore the blood test, delete the unsupported sentence.

**Do.** Point at the empty middle box, then at the three fixes. No chat on this slide.
:::

## Where the source comes from {#source-ladder}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.card .tint}
[1 · The primary source]{.t} The guideline, label or paper itself.
:::
::: {.card}
[2 · Your institution]{.t} Its formulary or guideline.
:::
::: {.card .dashed .fragment}
[Not a source]{.t} A second AI. Two drafts agreeing is not a check.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Asked for citations?
Open every one.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 30 sec]{.tag} A second tool agrees with the first. Verified? Type 1 for yes, 2 for no.
:::

::: notes
**1:30.** Where you look matters as much as whether you look. Best is the primary source: the guideline, the drug label, the paper itself. Next is your institution's formulary or guideline: local rules, which can differ from a published one, and what colleagues will hold you to. Now the poll, before the third rung shows. Then reveal it: a second AI is not a source. Two tools agreeing is two predictions, not a check, because neither was checked against anything. Asking a tool for citations does not fix this, because citations can be fabricated. Open every one and read the line it is supposed to support.

**Do.** Chat · 30 sec: "A second tool agrees with the first. Verified?" Show the count, click to reveal the third rung, then say no, and why. Do not ask who has used a second tool.
:::

## Effort follows the stakes {#stakes}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Wording, tone, formatting]{.node .same .fixed} [→]{.op} [Low: read it, fix what you would not say]{.node .grow}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[A summary of a document you have]{.node .out .fixed} [→]{.op} [Medium: each number and name against that document]{.node .grow}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[A dose, an allergy, a diagnosis, anything in a chart]{.node .change .fixed} [→]{.op} [The primary source, always]{.node .grow}
:::

[▲ How hard you check follows the stakes.]{.pointer}

[If you cannot find the source, treat the claim as wrong.]{.big}

Next: Lab Three. Its only tool is these five steps.

::: notes
**0:40.** How hard you check follows the stakes. Wording: read it and fix what you would not say. A summary of a document you have: check each number and name against that document. Doses, allergies, diagnoses and anything that goes into a chart: always the primary source, however routine it looks. That is the topic: tone tells you nothing, a step you do yourself does, and if you cannot find the source the claim counts as wrong. In a moment you swap your Lab One output with a partner and see what they catch.

**Do.** No vote; hand over to Lab Three, which uses only the five steps.
:::
